title: The Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment
note: From Copernicus (1543) to Newton (1687), thinkers replaced ancient authority with observation, experiment and mathematics. Enlightenment writers of the 1700s applied the same faith in reason to government and society, arguing for natural rights, limited government and the separation of powers.

read.title: Reason applied to nature and society
text: For centuries, educated Europeans followed ancient authorities such as Aristotle and Ptolemy, who placed Earth at the center of the universe. In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus argued that the sun was at the center instead. Johannes Kepler showed that planets travel in ellipses, and Galileo's telescope revealed moons circling Jupiter. In 1687 Isaac Newton explained these motions with a single law of gravitation that held on Earth and in the heavens. Thinkers such as Francis Bacon promoted a new method: observe, form a hypothesis, and test it by experiment.

If reason could uncover the laws of nature, many asked, could it also discover the laws of good government? John Locke argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that a government that violates them may be replaced. Montesquieu urged that power be divided among separate branches so that no one could become a tyrant. Voltaire attacked censorship and religious persecution, and Rousseau wrote of a social contract based on the general will.

These ideas spread through books, newspapers, coffeehouses and salons. Some monarchs, such as Catherine the Great, adopted reforms while keeping absolute power. Others faced revolutions led by people who had read Locke and Montesquieu.
